prelimsCapsule.coreConceptSummary: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India is the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department, acting as an agent of Parliament to ensure financial accountability of the executive. The powers, duties, and privileges of the CAG are derived from Articles 148-151 of the Constitution and significantly expanded and regulated by the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.
highYieldFacts: Fact 1: The CAG does not have executive authority to sanction expenditures; their role is strictly post-facto audit and attestation.
Fact 2: Under Article 148, the CAG is appointed by the President of India by warrant under his hand and seal, holding office for a term of 6 years or up to the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.
Fact 3: The CAG is not eligible for further office under the Government of India or any State government after ceasing to hold office (Article 148(4)).
Fact 4: The CAG's administrative expenses, including salaries and allowances, are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India (non-votable by Parliament).
Fact 5: The CAG Act of 1971 was amended in 1976 to relieve the CAG from the responsibility of compiling accounts for the Union government, though they continue to compile state accounts.
trapsAndElimination: Trap 1: Assuming CAG has pre-audit powers over government expenditure; CAG's primary mandate is post-audit (except in specific cases where requested or statutorily mandated).

Trap 2: Believing CAG can be removed by the President at will; removal requires an address by both Houses of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehavior or incapacity, similar to a Supreme Court judge.

mainsFramework.inDepthTheoryHtml:
Evolution and Constitutional Intent

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar famously remarked that the Comptroller and Auditor General of India shall be the most important officer under the Constitution of India, as his duties are far more important than those of even the judiciary. The framers of the Constitution envisioned the CAG as the ultimate guardian of the public purse, ensuring that public monies are spent in accordance with legislative authorization and financial propriety. The foundational architecture is enshrined in Chapter V of Part V of the Constitution, complemented by the comprehensive statutory framework of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.

Statutory Powers and Privileges under the 1971 Act

While the Constitution lays down the broad contours under Articles 148 to 151, the 1971 Act operationalizes the specific audit jurisdictions. The CAG possesses the power to inspect any office under the control of the Union or a State government, demand any records, books, papers, and documents, and question any public official. The privileges include complete independence of tenure, immunity from parliamentary debate on their conduct (except on a formal motion for removal), and the statutory right to access secret spending documents, subject to national security guidelines.

Contemporary Dynamics and Audit Scope

Over the decades, the scope of CAG audits has transcended traditional compliance and financial audit to encompass Performance Audit and Environmental Audit. Evaluating public policy efficacy—such as the audit of national schemes, public-private partnerships (PPPs), and autonomous bodies funded substantially from government revenues—has elevated the office into a major driver of good governance. However, challenges persist regarding the audit of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) receiving government grants, private distribution utilities in privatized sectors, and complex financial instruments.

dimensions.constitutional_or_legal: Tension between legislative intent and executive resistance regarding access to cabinet papers, commercial enterprise audits, and autonomous bodies.
dimensions.socio_economic: Ensuring that welfare expenditures reach the last mile by plugging leakages highlighted in CAG's performance audit reports.
dimensions.administrative_governance: Capacity constraints within the Indian Audit and Accounts Department (IAAD) and the transition toward digital/automated auditing tools (IT-enabled auditing).
dimensions.international_or_comparative: Alignment with INTOSAI (International Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions) standards and peer reviews to maintain global audit credibility.

modelMainsQA.modelAnswerHtml:
Introduction

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India, designated under Article 148, is the apex audit authority and the bulwark of the Indian democratic financial architecture. Described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the most important officer under the Constitution, the CAG ensures that the executive remains financially accountable to the legislature.

Constitutional Provisions and Statutory Powers

The powers and privileges of the CAG are meticulously designed to insulate the office from executive interference:

  • Constitutional Safeguards: Under Article 148, the CAG enjoys security of tenure akin to a Supreme Court judge, removable only through a joint address of Parliament. Expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, and post-retirement employment under the government is barred.
  • Statutory Mandate (CAG Act, 1971): The Act empowers the CAG to audit all receipts and expenditures of the Consolidated Fund of India and States, public undertakings, and corporations substantially financed by government revenues.
  • Access to Records: The CAG possesses sweeping powers to inspect any office, demand relevant documents, books, and confidential papers required for audit verification.

Evolution: From Compliance to Performance and Environmental Auditing

Traditionally focused on compliance and financial regularity (whether money was spent legally and authorized), the CAG's mandate has evolved dynamically:

  • Performance Audit: Assesses the 'economy, efficiency, and effectiveness' of government programs. Landmark performance audits (e.g., 2G Spectrum, coal block allocations) exposed systemic policy flaws and rent-seeking.
  • Environmental Audit: Evaluates ecological degradation, pollution control compliance, and sustainable development practices, aligning fiscal governance with inter-generational equity and climate goals.

Limitations in Functioning

Despite robust powers, structural bottlenecks remain: Post-Facto Nature: Audit occurs after expenditure has been incurred, limiting preventive action. Private Sector Scrutiny: Difficulty in auditing private entities operating under Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) without clear statutory backing. Legislative Backlog: Delay in examining CAG reports by Public Accounts Committees (PAC) dilutes the deterrent effect.

Conclusion

The CAG remains pivotal for fiscal transparency and constitutional morality. Empowering the IAAD with advanced data analytics (AI/Big Data) and ensuring time-bound legislative debate on CAG reports will fortify India's governance trajectory toward Viksit Bharat 2047.

practiceMCQs.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India:
1. The CAG is eligible for reappointment to the same office or any other office under the Government of India after the expiry of their term.
2. The administrative expenses of the office of the CAG are votable by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceMCQs.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: Article 148(4) explicitly bars the CAG from holding any further office under the Government of India or any State government after retirement. Statement 2 is incorrect: The administrative expenses, including salaries, allowances, and pensions of persons serving in that office, are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India and are non-votable.

practiceMCQs.question: With reference to the powers of the CAG under the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, which of the following bodies fall within the audit jurisdiction of the CAG?
options: All bodies and authorities substantially financed from the revenues of the Union or States
Government companies as defined under the Companies Act
Authorities and bodies financed from loans provided by the Consolidated Fund
practiceMCQs.explanation: Under sections 14, 19, and 20 of the CAG's (DPC) Act, 1971, the CAG's audit jurisdiction extends to government companies, corporations, and authorities/bodies that receive substantial financial assistance by way of grants or loans from the Consolidated Funds, ensuring comprehensive public sector financial oversight.
